stem: A urologist lowers the PSA cutoff for a biopsy referral from 4.0 to 2.5 ng/mL in a screening population of men aged 60. More men now test positive, fewer cancers are missed, and more biopsies show benign tissue.
oneliner: PSA cutoff lowered 4.0 → 2.5: fewer missed cancers, more benign biopsies → PPV and NPV?
ask: How do the predictive values change?

whyNot.A: Fewer cancers are missed, so **NPV rises**; more benign biopsies means **PPV falls**
whyNot.B: More benign biopsies means more false positives, so **PPV cannot rise**
whyNot.C: Fewer missed cancers means fewer false negatives, so **NPV rises**
whyNot.D: The cutoff changes who is called positive, so **both predictive values move**

why: A lower cutoff calls more men positive, so **sensitivity rises and specificity falls**. False negatives fall, so **NPV rises**; false positives rise, so **PPV falls**.

idea.rule: Lower the cutoff: sensitivity and NPV up, specificity and PPV down. Raise it: the reverse.
also: Screening tests use a low cutoff to rule disease out
Confirmatory tests use a high cutoff to rule disease in
A cutoff change moves along one ROC curve

stem: A troponin assay for myocardial infarction is plotted as an ROC curve with sensitivity on the y-axis and 1 − specificity on the x-axis. Five cutoffs are marked from point 1 (lower left) to point 5 (upper right), rising and moving right at each step. A confirmatory cutoff with the fewest false positives is needed.
oneliner: ROC of troponin cutoffs, points 1 (lower left) to 5 (upper right), need fewest false positives → which point?
ask: Which point gives the highest specificity?

whyNot.A: This upper-right point has the **highest sensitivity but the most false positives**
whyNot.B: Lies **to the right of points 1 and 2**, so it has more false positives
whyNot.C: Further right than point 3, so **more false positives**
whyNot.E: Lies **to the right of point 1**, so it has more false positives

why: Specificity = 1 − the x-axis value, so the point **furthest left** has the highest specificity. Moving up and right raises sensitivity but adds false positives; the lower-left point trades sensitivity for **fewest false positives**.

idea.rule: On an ROC curve, up and right = more sensitive, less specific; down and left = less sensitive, more specific.
also: Top-left corner is the best overall balance
The diagonal line means a useless test
A higher area under the curve means a better test overall

stem: A test validated in a referral clinic is used unchanged, with the same cutoff, in population screening where the disease is 10 times rarer.
oneliner: Same test, same cutoff, disease 10 times rarer → what changes?
ask: What happens when the test is moved to the lower-prevalence population?

whyNot.B: Sensitivity belongs to the test and **does not depend on prevalence**
whyNot.C: Specificity belongs to the test and **does not depend on prevalence**
whyNot.D: Fewer true cases among positives means **PPV falls**
whyNot.E: With fewer diseased people, a negative is more often right, so **NPV rises**

why: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test and stay the same. With fewer diseased people, a larger share of positives are false, so **PPV falls**, and a larger share of negatives are true, so **NPV rises**.
chain: True positives fall, false positives stay

idea.rule: Prevalence ↓: PPV ↓, NPV ↑. Prevalence ↑: PPV ↑, NPV ↓. Sensitivity and specificity do not change.
also: Screening a low-risk population gives many false positives
Testing a high-risk clinic population raises PPV
Likelihood ratios are also independent of prevalence

stem: Investigators triple a trial from 500 to 1500 patients and keep alpha at 0.05. The earlier result was p = 0.10, not significant, and the expected effect size is unchanged.
oneliner: Trial n tripled 500 → 1500, alpha 0.05 kept, same effect size → type I error, type II error, power?
ask: How do the error rates and power change?

whyNot.A: Alpha is **kept at 0.05**, so type I error does not change
whyNot.B: Alpha is **fixed**, so type I error does not rise
whyNot.D: A larger n **lowers** type II error and raises power
whyNot.E: A larger n never lowers power, and alpha stays at 0.05

answer: Type I unchanged; type II down; power up
why: Alpha is chosen in advance, so **type I error stays 5%**. More patients shrink the standard error, which lowers **type II error** and raises **power** for the same effect size.
chain: Easier to detect the same effect

idea.rule: Larger n: power up, beta down, CI narrower; alpha is set by the investigator and does not change.
also: Power rises with a larger effect size
Power falls with a larger SD
Power = 1 − beta

stem: A journal requires p < 0.01 instead of p < 0.05 for a planned trial whose sample size is fixed.
oneliner: Alpha 0.05 → 0.01, same sample size → type I error, type II error, power?
ask: How do the error rates and power change?

whyNot.A: A stricter threshold **lowers** type I error
whyNot.C: Type II error up means power is **down**, not up
whyNot.D: At fixed n a stricter alpha makes a real effect **harder** to detect
whyNot.E: Alpha is exactly what changed, so **type I error changes**

answer: Type I down; type II up; power down
why: A smaller alpha means a **lower false-positive rate**. With the same sample size, a larger effect is needed to reach p < 0.01, so real effects are missed more often: **beta rises and power falls**.

idea.rule: At fixed n, alpha and beta trade off: lower alpha means higher beta and lower power.
also: Raising n lets both errors fall together
Multiple-comparison corrections lower alpha per test and cost power
A two-sided test has less power than a one-sided test at the same alpha (effect in the tested direction)

stem: A 60-year-old man takes his own blood pressure and reports the mean of 4 readings, not 20. The standard deviation of the individual readings is 8 mmHg in both sets.
oneliner: 60M + home BP mean of 4 instead of 20 readings, SD 8 mmHg → SD, SE, CI width?
ask: How do the SD of the readings, the standard error and the confidence interval change with fewer readings?

whyNot.A: SE = SD/√n **rises** when n falls (1.79 to 4.0)
whyNot.B: Unchanged SD does not keep SE fixed, because **SE depends on n**
whyNot.C: The SD of the readings is **stated to be 8 mmHg in both sets**
whyNot.E: The SD is **8 mmHg in both sets**, so it does not fall

answer: SD unchanged; SE up; CI wider
why: SD describes the spread of readings and does not depend on n. **SE = SD/√n** rises from 8/√20 = 1.79 to 8/√4 = **4.0** mmHg, so the 95% CI (about ±2 SE) is **wider**.

idea.rule: SE = SD/√n: smaller n raises SE and widens the CI; SD does not change with n.
also: Quadrupling n halves the SE
Larger n narrows the CI and raises power
SD describes data; SE describes the precision of the mean

stem: A health department lowers the HbA1c cutoff that defines diabetes from 6.5% to 6.0%. The population and the biology of the disease have not changed, but more people now meet the definition.
oneliner: HbA1c cutoff for diabetes 6.5% → 6.0%, population and biology unchanged → incidence and prevalence?
ask: How do measured incidence and prevalence change?

whyNot.A: More people meeting the definition also **raises the number of existing cases**
whyNot.B: More people newly meeting the definition **raises new cases** too
whyNot.D: A looser definition **adds** cases, it does not remove them
whyNot.E: More people qualify, so **both counts rise**

why: A looser definition classifies **more people as cases**, both existing ones (prevalence) and newly detected ones (incidence). The rise is a measurement artifact, not a real change in disease.

idea.rule: Broadening a case definition raises measured incidence and prevalence without a real change in disease.
also: Better screening finds more cases
Lowering the hypertension or cholesterol threshold increases the number labelled as patients
A stricter definition lowers both

stem: A new screening program for lung cancer starts and treatment is unchanged. Tumors are now diagnosed about 2 years earlier, and their growth rate and the incidence of lung cancer are unchanged. Five-year survival, measured from the time of diagnosis, rises from 15% to 25%, while the age-specific death rate from lung cancer is unchanged.
oneliner: Lung cancer screening, diagnosis 2 years earlier, same tumor growth and incidence, 5-year survival 15% → 25%, death rate unchanged → explanation?
ask: Which best explains the rise in 5-year survival?

options.E: Diagnosis is earlier but death is not later

whyNot.A: The **death rate is unchanged**, so there is no mortality benefit
whyNot.D: That is length-time bias; the stem says **tumor growth rate is unchanged**

why: Screening moves the **time of diagnosis earlier** while death occurs when it always would, so survival from diagnosis lengthens. This is **lead-time bias**; only a fall in the **mortality rate** shows true benefit.
chain: Death occurs at the same time

idea.rule: Screening can raise survival from diagnosis without changing mortality (lead-time bias); judge benefit by mortality.
also: Length-time bias: screening picks up slow, less lethal tumors
Overdiagnosis adds cases that would never have caused harm
Randomized trials compare mortality, not survival after diagnosis

stem: Nine serum creatinine values (mg/dL) are 0.8, 0.8, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3. A lab error is found and one of the 0.8 values is re-entered as 1.1.
oneliner: Creatinine values 0.8 ×3, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1 ×2, 1.2, 1.3; one 0.8 becomes 1.1 → mean, median, mode?
ask: What happens to the mean, median and mode?

whyNot.B: The 5th value moves from 1.0 to 1.1 and the most frequent value changes, so **median and mode move**
whyNot.C: The most frequent value changes from 0.8 (×3) to **1.1 (×3)**
whyNot.D: The middle (5th) value changes from 1.0 to 1.1, so **the median moves too**
whyNot.E: Raising one value **cannot lower** the median or the mode

why: The sum rises from 9.0 to 9.3, so the **mean** goes from 1.000 to 1.033. Re-sorted, the 5th value is **1.1** instead of 1.0, and 1.1 now appears three times, replacing 0.8 as the **mode**.

idea.rule: Raising one value always raises the mean; median and mode change only if the middle or most frequent value changes.
also: An extreme outlier shifts the mean far more than the median
Mean = median = mode in a normal distribution
Right-skewed data: mean > median > mode

stem: Hospital lengths of stay in days for five patients are 2, 3, 3, 4 and 5. A sixth patient with a stay of 30 days is added.
oneliner: Stays 2, 3, 3, 4, 5 days; a 30-day stay added → which summary is least affected?
ask: Which measure is least affected by the added patient?

whyNot.A: Mean rises from 3.4 to **7.8 days**, pulled by the 30-day value
whyNot.C: The 30-day value is far from the center, so **SD rises sharply**
whyNot.E: Variance is SD squared, so the 30-day value **raises it even more** than the SD

why: The mean rises from 17/5 = 3.4 to 47/6 = **7.8** days and the SD and range balloon. The **median** moves only from 3 to (3 + 4)/2 = **3.5**, because it depends on rank, not on how extreme the largest value is.
chain: SD and range use the extremes: large rise

idea.rule: The median resists outliers; the mean, SD and range do not.
also: Use the median for skewed data such as length of stay or income
Mode is unaffected by an outlier unless it changes the most frequent value
Mean is pulled toward the tail of a skewed distribution

stem: Two glucose analyzers are each run 20 times on the same control sample. Both give the same mean value. The coefficient of variation is 3.5% for method I and 2.5% for method II.
oneliner: Two glucose analyzers, 20 repeats, same mean, CV 3.5% vs 2.5% → which statement is correct?

whyNot.A: Higher CV means **more scatter** in repeat results, so method I is less precise
whyNot.B: Accuracy needs the **true value**, which the stem does not give
whyNot.C: Accuracy needs the **true value**; scatter alone shows precision only
whyNot.D: Precision depends only on the **scatter of repeat results**, so no true value is needed

why: CV = SD/mean, so with the same mean a lower CV means **less scatter in repeat measurements**, which is greater **precision** (reliability). Accuracy is closeness to the true value and cannot be judged from repeats alone.
chain: Method II is more precise; accuracy still unknown

idea.rule: Precision = reproducibility (low random error, low CV); accuracy = closeness to the true value (low systematic error).
also: Reliability and precision describe the same property
Calibration against a reference standard tests accuracy
A biased but tight method is precise yet inaccurate

stem: Smoking carries a relative risk of 10 for disease X in two towns. In nonsmokers, the risk is 1 per 1000 in town A and 5 per 1000 in town B.
oneliner: RR 10 for smoking in two towns; nonsmoker risk 1/1000 (A) vs 5/1000 (B) → how do AR and NNH compare?
ask: Which statement about the two towns is correct?

options.A: Equal attributable risk in both towns
options.B: Higher relative risk in town B
options.C: Higher number needed to harm in town B
options.D: Larger AR and smaller NNH in town B
options.E: Lower attributable risk in town B

whyNot.A: Equal RR does not mean equal AR: **9 per 1000 in A vs 45 per 1000 in B**
whyNot.C: Larger AR means **smaller** NNH: about 22 in B vs 111 in A
whyNot.E: AR is **45 per 1000 in B**, above 9 per 1000 in A

answer: AR larger and NNH smaller in town B
why: Smokers' risk is 10 per 1000 in A and 50 per 1000 in B. AR = 10 − 1 = **9 per 1000** (NNH 1/0.009 = 111) in A and 50 − 5 = **45 per 1000** (NNH 1/0.045 = 22) in B.

idea.rule: At the same RR, a higher baseline risk gives a larger attributable risk and a smaller NNH.
also: Same relative risk reduction gives a smaller NNT in high-risk patients
RR measures strength of association, AR measures public health impact
Statins help high-risk patients more in absolute terms

stem: A meta-analysis pools 8 small randomized trials of a drug. Each trial has a confidence interval that crosses 1, and the point estimates all sit near RR 0.8.
oneliner: Meta-analysis of 8 small RCTs, each CI crosses 1, RR about 0.8 each → effect of pooling?
ask: What is the main effect of pooling these trials?

options.A: Pooled CI wider than any single trial
options.B: Lower power than the largest trial
options.D: Removal of bias in the included trials

whyNot.A: Pooling raises total n, so the CI **narrows**
whyNot.B: More patients in total **raise** power above any single trial
whyNot.D: Pooling **does not remove** bias in the individual trials
whyNot.E: The pooled analysis is **one test** at the chosen alpha

why: Pooling adds the patients of all trials, which **reduces the standard error**, narrows the CI and **raises power**. Bias in the individual trials is carried into the pooled estimate, not removed.

idea.rule: Pooling raises precision and power but cannot fix bias in the included studies.
also: Heterogeneity (high I²) limits how far trials should be pooled
Funnel plot asymmetry suggests publication bias
Fixed-effect and random-effects models weigh trials differently

stem: A randomized, double-blind trial enrolls only nonsmoking men aged 40 to 50 who have no other illness. The investigators then tighten the eligibility rules even further.
oneliner: RCT, only healthy nonsmoking men 40-50, eligibility tightened further, randomized and blinded → effect on validity?
ask: How do internal and external validity change as eligibility narrows?

whyNot.A: A more uniform sample means **less confounding and noise**, so internal validity does not fall
whyNot.C: Internal validity does rise, but a narrower sample is **less** like the general population, so external validity **falls**
whyNot.D: The sample now looks **less** like the general population, so external validity cannot rise
whyNot.E: Narrower eligibility changes the sample, so **both** validities move; neither stays put

answer: Internal validity rises and external validity falls
why: A uniform sample removes between-patient differences, so the result is **more trustworthy for the people studied** (internal validity up). The same restriction means **women, smokers, older and sicker patients** are not represented, so the result **generalizes less** (external validity down).
chain: Fewer confounders and less variability: internal validity rises
Fewer kinds of patients represented: external validity falls

idea.rule: Strict inclusion criteria buy internal validity at the cost of external validity.
also: Pragmatic trials with broad enrollment gain generalizability but accept more noise
Run-in periods that exclude nonadherent patients
Single-center trials in highly selected volunteers
Explanatory (efficacy) trials versus real-world effectiveness studies

stem: A case-control study asks about diet with a food-frequency questionnaire that misreports intake to the same degree in cases and in controls. The true odds ratio for the dietary exposure is 3.0.
oneliner: Case-control, diet questionnaire misreports equally in cases and controls, true OR 3.0 → direction of the measured OR?
ask: How will the measured odds ratio differ from the true value?

options.A: It is biased away from the null (above 3.0)
options.B: It is unaffected by the misclassification
options.C: It is reversed to a protective value (below 1)
options.D: It is biased toward the null (between 1 and 3.0)

whyNot.A: Equal error in both groups **blurs** the contrast; it does not exaggerate it
whyNot.B: Misclassification **does** distort the estimate, not just precision
whyNot.C: Reversal needs **differential**, strongly directed error; equal error only dilutes
whyNot.E: Equal misclassification moves the **point estimate** itself, not only the interval

answer: Biased toward the null (OR falls from 3.0 toward 1)
why: Error that is **equal in cases and controls** (nondifferential) mixes exposed people into the unexposed group and vice versa. The two groups look **more alike**, so the measured association is **pulled toward the null**.
chain: Misreporting is the same in both groups
Some exposed people are labelled unexposed and the reverse
Exposure rates in cases and controls move closer together

idea.rule: Nondifferential (random) misclassification biases toward the null; differential misclassification can go either way.
also: Recall bias is usually differential and can exaggerate or hide an effect
Equal error in measuring an exposure in cases and controls underestimates a true OR
Imprecise outcome definition equal in both arms dilutes a trial effect
Interviewer bias applied unequally is differential
